positions.commentary: The speaker notes that a large-cap stock like Facebook (Meta) can lose hundreds of billions in market cap in a single event, arguing this demonstrates market inefficiency and inelasticity rather than active repricing.
The speaker mentions Cisco reporting a slowdown in customer order activity as an example of information that passive investors ignore because they assume the last price is correct.

thesis: This episode argues that large-cap stocks like Meta can experience massive market cap losses in single events due to market inefficiency and inelasticity, rather than active repricing. It further suggests that passive investors ignore specific fundamental information, such as Cisco's slowdown in customer orders, because they assume the last traded price is always correct.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that a large-cap stock like Facebook (Meta) can lose hundreds of billions in market cap in a single event, arguing this demonstrates market inefficiency and inelasticity rather than active repricing.
claims.quote: one of the sort of armchair critiques I see all the time. People throw this one at you on Twitter, I see it quite frequently, is they'll point to a big mega-cap stock. like Facebook meta, down 20% after earnings. And they'll say, see, passive isn't supporting this. This is clearly an active repricing.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Cisco reporting a slowdown in customer order activity as an example of information that passive investors ignore because they assume the last price is correct.
claims.quote: Vanguard receives no incremental information when Facebook has a terrible quarter or when Cisco reports that, you know, there's a slowdown in customer order activity. There's nobody even paying attention to that.
